titleStmt.title: To Harriet Shaw Weaver. Monday, 8 January 1923
titleStmt.author: James Joyce

seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p:
I am very sorry indeed to hear that you have so much and so dangerous illness in the house. I hoped you would have had a peaceful time there, snowed up as I saw by the papers. I shall try to weary you as little as possible and hope the danger you spoke of is now past. My own insignificant operation is put off till the 16.– the first one. I shall send you Miss Deutsch’s article tomorrow. The only request I have to make is that whenever you have time you ask Mr Rodker to send a stamped press copy to:
Mr Bernard Gilbert (he is reviewing the book for the Leeds Mercury)
c/o Authors’ Club
2 Whitehall Court
London SW1
I could write myself but for many reasons I prefer not to that is unless you tell me expressly that you prefer me to correspond directly with him.

closer.salute: With every hope that things are now better with you and kindest regards

div.note: Harriet Shaw Weaver was at Castle Park, the family house in Frodsham, where “the Misses Wright” (as they are referred to on the envelope of this letter) lived, two unmarried aunts Harriet Elizabeth and Emily Priscilla Wright (sisters of Weaver’s mother, Mary Berry Wright). Aunt Emily died on 4 January 1923; Aunt Harriet in 1931 (Jane Lidderdale and Mary Nicholson, Dear Miss Weaver: Harriet Shaw Weaver 1876-1961 (New York: The Viking Press, 1970), 213-4; 308).

As per New York endocrinologist Dr Louis Berman’s advice in July 1922 and Dr Borsch’s similar recommendation in October 1922, JJ would undergo complete dental extraction and a subsequent sphincterectomy in early 1923. With Dr Borsch’s consent, JJ ultimately postponed the operation. On 4 April 1923, six or seven of JJ’s decayed teeth were extracted, with the rest of them a few days later. After his seventeen tooth extractions, Borsch performed a sphincterectomy in three parts (April 3, 15, and 26) (JJ 536-7; 543).
Babette Deutsch. "On Ulysses." Literary Review of the New York Evening Post, (2 December 1922): 281.

JJ saw Gilbert, probably in mid-January and made notes from two of his novels. However, Gilbert did not review Ulysses until 1925 and not in the Leeds Mercury but, very negatively, in Chesterton's G. K.’s Weekly and The Double Dealer. See Robbert-Jan Henkes, "Before King Roderick Became Publican in Chapelizod: The Origins of the Origins of Finnegans Wake." Genetic Joyce Studies, 12 (Spring 2012).
